newsitem.title: GERMANY: INSTANT VIEW - German state CPI, import price data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - German state CPI, import price data.

text.p: Following are reactions from economists to German March consumer inflation data from the states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Hesse and to February pan-German import prices.

North Rhine-Westphalia's consumer price index for March fell 0.2 percent month-on-month and rose 1.8 percent year-on-year against respective February gains of 0.5 percent and 2.0 percent. Hesse's March CPI fell 0.1 percent and rose 1.4 percent year-on-year, compared with respective February rates of 0.3 percent and 1.5 percent.
German import prices in February rose 0.5 percent month-on-month and rose 3.0 percent year-on-year.

STEPHAN RIEKE, BHF-BANK: "The import prices are for February and therefore still reflect the impact of the rise in the dollar and in oil prices. So the rise in import prices is not very surprising as we had similar growth in consumer and producer prices in the first two months of 1997. The consumer price data for March are quite satisfactory. We expected a clear weakening from February but we did not expect a month-on-month decline in prices. There are three factors dampening price growth. A decline in the price of heating oil, in package holidays and in seasonal foods. Overall we expect west German consumer prices to be flat or down 0.1 percent in March for a year-on-year rate of 1.6 percent. This shows that the strong price rises in January and February did not set a trend for the whole year."

GERHARD GREBE, BANK JULIUS BAER, FRANKFURT: "The inflation situation is better than we expected. On a monthly basis we expected a rise of +0.1 percent, but instead it fell 0.1 percent. The main reason is the fall in heating oil prices and lower fruit and vegetable prices.
"In January and February the weather played a big role on the seasonally-affected indicators. In February package tours lifted inflation rates, for example. But these factors are now gone.

"+1.6 percent in March for West Germany, after +1.7 percent in February and +1.9 percent in January shows a clear decline in inflation levels. I think we are looking at +1.5 for the middle of the year on a year-on-year basis, or below that level.

"I don't think the Bundesbank is going to change interest rates this year. There are no inflationary dangers in the economy. There is no need for the Bundesbank to raise rates, but they won't sink them either in order to keep the dollar stable," said Grebe.

"Import prices rose in connection with the dollar. These are one month behind -- the figures are for February. The rise of the dollar was mostly in January and there was also a strong rise in heating oil and oil prices then," said Grebe.
